screens.title: BGP Path Attributes and Route Selection Process
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how Border Gateway Protocol uses path attributes to make precise routing decisions. BGP is policy-driven: routing choices are not decided by a single metric but by an ordered evaluation of attributes such as next-hop reachability, local preference, AS path length, origin type, MED, and whether a route was learned via eBGP or iBGP. Understanding these attributes is essential for traffic engineering and avoiding unexpected routing behavior. We'll use common Junos examples to show how LOCAL_PREF affects outbound selection, how MED suggests preferred entry points to a neighbor, and how AS_PATH prevents loops and biases path length. You will also see configuration patterns—import and export policies, AS-path prepending, and LOCAL_PREF assignment—that operators use to influence traffic. By the end you should be able to read route attributes with Junos show commands, predict which path Junos will pick, and create simple policies to change that decision. Think of BGP attributes as a ranked checklist: if the first test fails, Junos moves to the next. That order is what gives you predictable control when you tune policies.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will identify the most common BGP path attributes and explain how they affect routing decisions in Junos. You will be comfortable reading AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, LOCAL_PREF, MED, and ORIGIN values with show commands and understand why next-hop reachability is the first gating check. You will also step through Junos' best path selection sequence so you can predict which route will be chosen when attributes differ. Finally, you will learn to write simple import and export routing policies—setting local preference, adding MED values, and prepending AS numbers—to influence inbound and outbound traffic. Each objective emphasizes practical checks: verifying next-hop reachability in the routing table, confirming that LOCAL_PREF changes only affect iBGP peers, and ensuring you apply MED to the correct neighbor. These skills help prevent common mistakes like applying import policies when export policies are intended or ignoring IGP reachability for iBGP next-hops. Together these objectives prepare you to read, reason about, and safely adjust BGP route selection on Juniper devices.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: In practice, mastering BGP attributes lets you shape traffic predictably across multiple ISPs. You will learn to prefer one eBGP link for outbound traffic by raising LOCAL_PREF across your AS, ensuring all internal routers pick the desired exit. You will also learn to influence an adjacent ISP's choices by advertising different MED values or by prepending your AS number to make certain paths appear longer. These manipulations are not arbitrary; they must be verified using Junos show commands and tested to avoid blackholing or loops. You'll also internalize the distinction between attributes that are internal-only, like LOCAL_PREF, and attributes that travel to neighbors, like AS_PATH and NEXT_HOP. Finally, you'll practice common troubleshooting checks such as confirming next-hop reachability and reviewing IGP cost for iBGP next-hops. These practical outcomes reduce surprise routing changes and let you communicate changes clearly to peers and operators.

keyIdea.title: Operational benefit
keyIdea.text: Attribute control turns routing policy into predictable traffic engineering rather than guesswork.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Practical Outcomes
Apply LOCAL_PREF for outbound control
Set LOCAL_PREF higher for routes from your preferred ISP so internal routers prefer that exit. This affects all iBGP peers and provides a single point of control.
Use MED to suggest inbound entry
Advertise lower MED on the link you want the neighbor to prefer. Remember MED is a suggestion and is compared per-adjacent AS by default on Junos.
Prepend AS_PATH for remote deterrence
When you want a remote AS to avoid a path, prepend your AS to make that path appear longer and less preferred.
Verification steps
Always verify with show route protocol bgp detail and check next-hop reachability to avoid misapplied policies or unreachable next-hops.

screens.title: BGP and Path Attributes — a definition
screens.narratorSegment: BGP carries a set of path attributes with every route. These attributes are descriptive metadata: they explain how a route was learned, which routers the route has passed through, and how other routers should prefer or avoid the route. Unlike interior routing protocols that use a simple metric to choose the best route, BGP performs an ordered evaluation of attributes to make a single, deterministic best-path decision. This design gives network operators policy control: by changing attributes before export or on import, you influence route selection without changing physical topology. A concrete example is comparing two routes to the same prefix: one route might have a higher LOCAL_PREF but a shorter AS_PATH, and Junos will evaluate LOCAL_PREF before AS_PATH so the higher LOCAL_PREF wins. A common misconception is to treat MED like LOCAL_PREF; they are not interchangeable. LOCAL_PREF is internal — it controls how your AS sends traffic out — while MED is a suggestion you give to a neighbor to influence how they send traffic into your AS. Remember also that some attributes are well-known and mandatory, such as NEXT_HOP and AS_PATH, while others are optional. The essential takeaway is that attributes are your policy knobs; use them carefully and verify with route detail commands.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Path attributes are the ranked metadata BGP uses to select and influence routes; they are the levers for policy-driven routing.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Path Attributes
What is a path attribute?
Descriptive metadata carried in BGP updates used to decide which route is selected.
Well-known mandatory
Examples: AS_PATH and NEXT_HOP. These are always present and are fundamental for loop prevention and forwarding.
Well-known discretionary
LOCAL_PREF is exchanged inside an AS to influence outbound decisions.
Optional
MED is optional and not transitive; it advises an adjacent AS about preferred entry.
Key Takeaway

Attributes are policy controls and must be read and tested with show route commands before trusting behavior.

Concrete example
Suppose two routes to 203.0.113.0/24 arrive. Route A has LOCAL_PREF 200 and AS_PATH length 3. Route B has LOCAL_PREF 100 and AS_PATH length 1. Junos prefers the higher LOCAL_PREF even though AS_PATH is shorter on Route B.
Misconception check
Do not assume MED and LOCAL_PREF behave the same. MED suggests an external preference; LOCAL_PREF is authoritative inside your AS.
Try this verification
show route protocol bgp 203.0.113.0/24 detail
This command reveals attributes and the chosen best path for the prefix.

screens.title: AS_PATH: purpose and behavior
screens.narratorSegment: AS_PATH is a well-known mandatory attribute containing the ordered list of autonomous systems a route traversed. Its two most important operational roles are loop prevention and path-length comparison. Loop prevention is simple: if a BGP speaker sees its own AS in the AS_PATH, it discards the route. For preference, Junos treats shorter AS_PATHs as more desirable after LOCAL_PREF checks have been performed. A concrete example: if a route comes with AS_PATH [65010 65020] and another with [65030], and both have equal LOCAL_PREF, the path with AS_PATH length one is preferred. Operators often use AS-path prepending to intentionally lengthen the AS_PATH when advertising to a peer, making that export less attractive to remote networks. The common pitfall here is overusing prepending without verification — excessive prepending can push traffic through unexpected intermediaries or create asymmetry. Always verify the effect by asking the peer to show received routes or by using public BGP looking glass tools. On Junos, you implement prepending in an export policy with an as-path-prepend action. The closing takeaway: use AS_PATH and prepending as a coarse remote steering tool and verify changes from the remote perspective.

keyIdea.title: AS_PATH summary
keyIdea.text: AS_PATH records traversed AS numbers; shorter paths are preferred and prepending increases perceived length.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › AS_PATH
AS_PATH behavior
Records AS numbers a route passed through. Used to prevent loops and to prefer shorter paths after LOCAL_PREF is evaluated.
Loop prevention
If a router sees its AS in AS_PATH, it rejects the update to avoid a loop.
Path preference
Between equal LOCAL_PREFs, Junos prefers the shorter AS_PATH.
Prepending
Add your AS multiple times on export to make the path less attractive to remote networks.
Configuration snippet (export prepending)
set policy-options policy-statement PREPEND_AS_TO_ISP_B term 1 then as-path-prepend "65000 65000"
set protocols bgp group TO_ISP_B export PREPEND_AS_TO_ISP_B
This makes the advertised AS_PATH look longer to peers of ISP B.
Misconception
Prepending guarantees no diversion. It only changes perceived path length; the remote AS has other attributes and policies that may override your suggestion.

screens.title: NEXT_HOP and reachability
screens.narratorSegment: NEXT_HOP is a well-known mandatory attribute that tells routers which IP address to forward packets to for a given prefix. The first criterion in Junos' best-path selection is that the NEXT_HOP must be reachable via an active route in the local routing table. If the next-hop is unreachable, the BGP route is considered invalid regardless of other attractive attributes. For eBGP neighbors, the next-hop is typically the peer's address. For iBGP paths, NEXT_HOP is usually preserved from the originating eBGP advertisement, which means internal routers require IGP routes to that next-hop. A practical example: an iBGP-learned route points to a next-hop on a remote eBGP peer; if the IGP lacks a path to that next-hop, the route will not become eligible. A common operational mistake is to forget to redistribute or provide IGP reachability to eBGP next-hops when using iBGP. Verify NEXT_HOP reachability with show route and trace the IGP path. The takeaway: always confirm next-hop reachability before changing other attributes; it is the gate that determines whether the rest of the best-path sequence even runs. NEXT_HOP and reachability means a route with an unreachable next-hop is discarded; ensure igp reachability for ibgp next-hops.. In practical terms, why next-hop reachability is the first gating check. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: NEXT_HOP gate
keyIdea.text: A route with an unreachable next-hop is discarded; ensure IGP reachability for iBGP next-hops.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › NEXT_HOP
NEXT_HOP reachability
The next-hop IP must be present in the routing table for the BGP path to be considered. This is the first check in Junos' selection algorithm.
eBGP behavior
NEXT_HOP is normally the directly connected peer address and is usually reachable by default.
iBGP behavior
iBGP preserves NEXT_HOP from eBGP peers. Internal routers must have an IGP route to that NEXT_HOP.
Verification commands
show route protocol bgp  detail
show route  detail
Check that the next-hop resolves to an active route before modifying other attributes.
Common mistake
Relying on iBGP without ensuring the IGP knows loopback next-hops. This leads to otherwise valid BGP paths being ignored.

screens.title: LOCAL_PREF: controlling outbound traffic
screens.narratorSegment: LOCAL_PREF is a well-known discretionary attribute exchanged only among iBGP peers in the same AS. Its role is to signal which exit point the local AS prefers for outbound traffic. A higher LOCAL_PREF value is preferred, and it is evaluated early in the Junos best-path selection sequence after next-hop reachability. For example, if your AS has two eBGP peers to different ISPs and you set LOCAL_PREF 200 on routes learned from ISP A and leave ISP B at the default 100, all routers in your AS will prefer ISP A as the exit point for those prefixes. Practically, you implement this by creating an import policy that assigns local-preference and applying it to the BGP group. Mistakes often stem from applying the policy on the wrong direction: LOCAL_PREF must be applied on import to influence how you accept routes, not on export. Another pitfall is thinking LOCAL_PREF affects how neighbors choose paths into your AS — it does not. That is the role of MED or AS-path prepending. The takeaway: LOCAL_PREF is your authoritative internal stick for choosing an exit; use import policies and verify with show route protocol bgp.

keyIdea.title: LOCAL_PREF control
keyIdea.text: LOCAL_PREF sets which exit your AS uses for outbound traffic; higher wins and is set with import policies.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › LOCAL_PREF
What LOCAL_PREF does
An iBGP-only attribute that determines which path the AS prefers for outbound traffic. Higher is preferred.
Example use
Set LOCAL_PREF 200 for routes from ISP A and 100 for ISP B so the AS prefers ISP A for outbound flows.
Configuration example
set policy-options policy-statement PREFER_ISP_A term 1 then local-preference 200
set protocols bgp group FROM_ISP_A import PREFER_ISP_A

set policy-options policy-statement PREFER_ISP_B term 1 then local-preference 100
set protocols bgp group FROM_ISP_B import PREFER_ISP_B
Apply these as import policies on the groups receiving routes from each ISP.
Misconception
LOCAL_PREF affects outbound selection inside your AS only; it does not directly influence how upstream peers route to you.

screens.title: MED: influencing inbound traffic
screens.narratorSegment: MED, the Multi-Exit Discriminator, is an optional, non-transitive attribute used to tell a neighboring AS which entry point into your AS it should prefer. Unlike LOCAL_PREF, which controls outbound traffic inside your AS, MED is a suggestion for the adjacent AS about inbound traffic. Lower MED values are preferred. MED is typically exchanged between eBGP neighbors and is compared only among routes learned from the same adjacent AS by default on Junos. A concrete scenario: if you have two links to the same ISP AS, advertise a lower MED on the link you want that ISP to use as the primary entry. On Junos you set MED with the metric action in a policy prior to export. A common mistake is expecting MED to override LOCAL_PREF; it cannot. MED only affects the remote AS's decision, and how the remote AS evaluates MED depends on its own policies and configuration. Also remember MED is not transitive, so it won't propagate further beyond the immediate neighbor. The practical takeaway is to use MED when you want to influence a specific neighbor's inbound choice, and always test by checking the neighbor's received routes or asking them to report the decision.

keyIdea.title: MED purpose
keyIdea.text: MED suggests which of your multiple entry points a neighboring AS should use; lower values are preferred.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › MED
What MED does
An optional attribute sent to a neighbor to suggest which entry point they should prefer when sending inbound traffic to your AS.
Comparison
LOCAL_PREF influences your AS; MED influences an adjacent AS. Use MED only when you want to affect the neighbor's decision.
Configuration example
set policy-options policy-statement PREFER_LINK1_INBOUND term 1 then metric 50
set protocols bgp group TO_ISP_LINK1 export PREFER_LINK1_INBOUND
Lower metric value suggests the ISP prefer this link when choosing how to send traffic to you.
Misconception
MED is a suggestion and applies per-adjacent AS; the neighbor may ignore it or compare MED differently depending on its configuration.

screens.title: ORIGIN attribute explained
screens.narratorSegment: ORIGIN indicates how a route entered BGP and serves as an early tie-breaker in the best-path selection. There are three origin codes: IGP, EGP, and Incomplete. IGP, marked as 'i', means the route was originated within the local AS using a network statement. EGP, 'e', is historical and rarely used. Incomplete, '?', indicates the route was redistributed into BGP from another source such as an IGP or static route. In Junos, the origin preference order is IGP first, then EGP, then Incomplete. This means that, after LOCAL_PREF and AS_PATH comparisons, a route tagged as IGP will beat one tagged as Incomplete. A practical example is when you redistribute static routes into BGP: those often become Incomplete and will be less preferred than routes that were originated via a BGP network statement. A common operator mistake is not understanding how redistribution changes origin and then being surprised when an internally originated route loses to an externally learned route. The takeaway: maintain clear origin semantics in your policy design and use explicit network statements when you want an IGP origin preference. ORIGIN attribute explained means origin signals how a route entered bgp; igp-originated routes are preferred over redistributed (incomplete) routes.. In practical terms, how origin type affects route preference. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › ORIGIN
Origin codes and preference
IGP (i) > EGP (e) > Incomplete (?). Origin is evaluated early in the sequence and breaks ties after AS_PATH checks in the standard order.
Practical note
Redistributed routes typically become Incomplete and will lose to IGP-originated BGP routes unless other attributes override.
Example
A route defined with a network statement in Junos is IGP-origin; a static redistributed into BGP is Incomplete. If attributes are otherwise equal, IGP-origin wins.
Misconception
Do not assume redistribution preserves origin preference. Explicit network origination is preferred when you need precedence.

screens.title: Junos BGP Best Path Selection
screens.narratorSegment: Junos follows a strict, step-by-step process to select a single best BGP path when multiple paths exist. The first check is next-hop reachability: if the next-hop is not in the routing table the path is discarded. Next, Junos compares LOCAL_PREF and prefers the path with the highest value, which is why operators use LOCAL_PREF to control outbound behavior. If LOCAL_PREF is equal, Junos prefers the shorter AS_PATH. If AS_PATH lengths are equal, the ORIGIN code is evaluated with preference order IGP, EGP, and then Incomplete. MED comes next: Junos prefers the lower MED but, by default, compares MED only among routes learned from the same adjacent AS. If MED is equal or not comparable, Junos prefers eBGP-learned paths over iBGP. For iBGP-learned routes, it then considers the IGP cost to reach the BGP next-hop and prefers the lower cost. Remaining tie-breakers are lowest Router ID and, finally, lowest peer IP address. A concrete example: two routes with equal LOCAL_PREF and reachable next-hops will be compared by AS_PATH length and origin next. A frequent misconception is that MED always wins over AS_PATH; it does not. The right sequence helps you predict outcomes and design policies accordingly.

keyIdea.text: Next-hop reachability gates the process, then LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH, ORIGIN, MED, eBGP over iBGP, IGP cost, Router ID, and peer IP.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Best Path Steps
1. Next-Hop Reachability
Path must have a reachable next-hop in the routing table or it is ignored.
2. LOCAL_PREF
Highest local preference wins; primary control for outbound selection.
3. AS_PATH Length
Shortest AS_PATH preferred when LOCAL_PREFs are equal.
4. ORIGIN
Prefer IGP < EGP < Incomplete.
5. MED
Lower MED preferred; typically compared per-adjacent AS on Junos.
6. eBGP over iBGP
Prefer routes learned from eBGP if attributes are equal.
7–9. IGP Cost, Router ID, Peer IP
IGP cost to BGP next-hop, lowest Router ID, then lowest peer IP are last tie-breakers.
Worked example
Two equal routes with reachable next-hops and equal LOCAL_PREF: compare AS_PATH length. If still equal, prefer IGP origin. If still equal, compare MED only if from same neighbor; otherwise prefer eBGP.
Misconception
Do not assume a single attribute always wins; follow the sequence to reason why a path was chosen.

screens.title: Manipulating attributes with Junos policies
screens.narratorSegment: Routing policies in Junos let you modify attributes at import or export time to control how routes are accepted or advertised. The direction matters: an import policy alters attributes of routes you receive before they enter your RIB, while an export policy changes attributes before you send routes to a neighbor. Use import policies to set LOCAL_PREF for routes learned from a peer so internal routers prefer or avoid that path. Use export policies to set MED or prepend AS numbers before advertising to a neighbor when you want to influence their decisions. For example, to prefer ISP A for outbound traffic, create an import policy that sets local-preference 200 and apply it to the group receiving routes from ISP A. To make ISP B less preferred externally, create an export policy that prepends your AS twice and apply it to the group for ISP B. A common operator error is applying a LOCAL_PREF change as an export action expecting remote peers to change their behavior — LOCAL_PREF is only exchanged internally, so it must be applied on import. Always validate policy effects with show route protocol bgp detail and, for export effects, ask the neighbor to run show route receive-protocol or check a looking glass if available. The operational lesson: direction and the attribute's scope determine which policy type to use.

keyIdea.title: Policy direction matters
keyIdea.text: Import policies set attributes you accept, export policies set attributes you announce. Choose direction based on attribute scope.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Policies
Import vs Export
Import policies shape the attributes of routes you accept; export policies shape attributes you send to peers. Apply LOCAL_PREF on import; MED or prepending on export.
Example: prefer ISP A
set policy-options policy-statement PREFER_ISP_A term 1 then local-preference 200
set protocols bgp group TO_ISP_A import PREFER_ISP_A
Example: make ISP B prefer another path
set policy-options policy-statement PREPEND_AS_TO_ISP_B term 1 then as-path-prepend "65000 65000"
set protocols bgp group TO_ISP_B export PREPEND_AS_TO_ISP_B
This makes your route appear longer to ISP B and remote peers that see that path.
Verification
Use show route protocol bgp <prefix> detail locally and request the neighbor's received-route view to confirm exported attribute changes.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Several repeatable mistakes cause unexpected BGP behavior. First, confusing LOCAL_PREF and MED leads operators to apply the wrong policy direction: LOCAL_PREF affects outbound decisions inside your AS and is set on import; MED is exported to neighbors to influence inbound choice. Second, failing to ensure IGP reachability to BGP next-hops causes iBGP-learned routes to be invalid even if attributes are attractive. Third, applying an import policy when you intended export will silently change attribute visibility and can cause route loss or asymmetry. Finally, excessive AS-path prepending without verification can shift traffic to unintended intermediate providers and make troubleshooting harder. For troubleshooting, start with next-hop verification: run show route protocol bgp detail and confirm the next-hop is present in the routing table. Then inspect LOCAL_PREF and AS_PATH in the same output to see why a different path may have been selected. If you changed export behavior, ask the neighbor to show their received routes or use a looking glass to validate the effect. The practical habit is to make single changes, verify with show outputs, and have rollback steps ready. That disciplined approach prevents prolonged outages or blackholes.

keyIdea.text: Check next-hop reachability first, then inspect LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH, MED and policy directions to find why a path was chosen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Troubleshooting
Common mistakes
  • Mixing up LOCAL_PREF (import) and MED (export).
  • Missing IGP route to iBGP NEXT_HOP.
  • Applying policies in the wrong direction.
  • Over-prepending AS_PATH without verification.
Debug workflow
1) Confirm next-hop with show route. 2) Inspect LOCAL_PREF and AS_PATH in show route protocol bgp <prefix> detail. 3) If export changed attributes, request the neighbor's received view.
Example verification
show route protocol bgp 192.0.2.0/24 detail
show route 203.0.113.1 detail

screens.title: Hands-on: Influencing inbound and outbound traffic
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on scenario asks you to influence outbound traffic toward ISP A and make ISP B prefer a different path into your network. The network has R1 in AS 65000 peered to R2 (ISP A, AS 100) and R3 (ISP B, AS 200). To prefer ISP A for outbound traffic, create an import policy on R1 that sets local-preference 200 for routes learned from R2, and ensure that policy is attached to the BGP group receiving routes from ISP A. For inbound control toward R3, create an export policy that prepends your AS twice so the path appears longer to ISP B and remote peers. The lesson includes the canonical Junos snippets: set policy-options policy-statement PREFER_ISP_A term 1 then local-preference 200 and set policy-options policy-statement PREPEND_AS_TO_ISP_B term 1 then as-path-prepend "65000 65000". Configure the BGP groups to use these policies on import or export as appropriate. After applying changes, verify with show route protocol bgp detail on R1 to confirm LOCAL_PREF and AS_PATH. Also check R3's received view via show route receive-protocol bgp if you can. A common error is forgetting to advertise the local prefix or forgetting to provide IGP reachability to next-hops; verify the static route or network configuration used to originate the test prefix. This exercise reinforces the import/export distinction and the verification steps.

keyIdea.text: Use import LOCAL_PREF to prefer ISP A outbound and export AS_PATH prepending to influence ISP B inbound; always verify with show commands.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Lab Walkthrough
Scenario summary
R1 (AS 65000) peers with R2 (ISP A, AS 100) and R3 (ISP B, AS 200). R1 advertises 192.168.100.0/24 to both ISPs. Goal: prefer R2 for outbound, make R3 prefer a less desired path inbound.
Step-by-step
  1. Create import policy PREFER_ISP_A to set local-preference 200 and attach to group from ISP A.
  2. Create export policy PREPEND_AS_TO_ISP_B to as-path-prepend "65000 65000" and attach to group to ISP B.
  3. Announce 192.168.100.0/24 via network or static routing and verify with show commands.
Junos configuration snippets
# Prefer ISP A for outbound
set policy-options policy-statement PREFER_ISP_A term 1 then local-preference 200
set protocols bgp group TO_ISP_A import PREFER_ISP_A

# Make ISP B see a longer path
set policy-options policy-statement PREPEND_AS_TO_ISP_B term 1 then as-path-prepend "65000 65000"
set protocols bgp group TO_ISP_B export PREPEND_AS_TO_ISP_B
Verification
Run show route protocol bgp <prefix> detail on R1 and ask R3 for show route receive-protocol bgp <R1_IP> to confirm the prepended AS_PATH.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These three concepts capture the essentials you will use daily. First, AS_PATH is both loop prevention and a length metric; shorter AS_PATHs are preferred after LOCAL_PREF. Keep these three in mind when you read show route output or design simple policies: verify next-hop before attribute comparisons, set LOCAL_PREF where you want to control internal exit selection, and use AS_PATH prepending carefully to influence remote choices. These quick reminders help you reason about why Junos picks one path instead of another and avoid common operational mistakes. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how Border Gateway Protocol uses path attributes to make precise routing decisions. BGP is policy-driven: routing choices are not decided by a single metric but by an ordered evaluation of attributes such as next-hop reachability, local preference, AS path length, origin type, MED, and whether a route was learned via eBGP or iBGP. Understanding these attributes is essential for traffic engineering and avoiding unexpected routing behavior. We'll use common Junos examples to show how LOCAL_PREF affects outbound selection, how MED suggests preferred entry points to a neighbor, and how AS_PATH prevents loops and biases path length. You will also see configuration patterns—import and export policies, AS-path prepending, and LOCAL_PREF assignment—that operators use to influence traffic. By the end you should be able to read route attributes with Junos show commands, predict which path Junos will pick, and create simple policies to change that decision. Think of BGP attributes as a ranked checklist: if the first test fails, Junos moves to the next. That order is what gives you predictable control when you tune policies.

By the end of this chapter you will identify the most common BGP path attributes and explain how they affect routing decisions in Junos. You will be comfortable reading AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, LOCAL_PREF, MED, and ORIGIN values with show commands and understand why next-hop reachability is the first gating check. You will also step through Junos' best path selection sequence so you can predict which route will be chosen when attributes differ. Finally, you will learn to write simple import and export routing policies—setting local preference, adding MED values, and prepending AS numbers—to influence inbound and outbound traffic. Each objective emphasizes practical checks: verifying next-hop reachability in the routing table, confirming that LOCAL_PREF changes only affect iBGP peers, and ensuring you apply MED to the correct neighbor. These skills help prevent common mistakes like applying import policies when export policies are intended or ignoring IGP reachability for iBGP next-hops. Together these objectives prepare you to read, reason about, and safely adjust BGP route selection on Juniper devices.

In practice, mastering BGP attributes lets you shape traffic predictably across multiple ISPs. You will learn to prefer one eBGP link for outbound traffic by raising LOCAL_PREF across your AS, ensuring all internal routers pick the desired exit. You will also learn to influence an adjacent ISP's choices by advertising different MED values or by prepending your AS number to make certain paths appear longer. These manipulations are not arbitrary; they must be verified using Junos show commands and tested to avoid blackholing or loops. You'll also internalize the distinction between attributes that are internal-only, like LOCAL_PREF, and attributes that travel to neighbors, like AS_PATH and NEXT_HOP. Finally, you'll practice common troubleshooting checks such as confirming next-hop reachability and reviewing IGP cost for iBGP next-hops. These practical outcomes reduce surprise routing changes and let you communicate changes clearly to peers and operators.

BGP carries a set of path attributes with every route. These attributes are descriptive metadata: they explain how a route was learned, which routers the route has passed through, and how other routers should prefer or avoid the route. Unlike interior routing protocols that use a simple metric to choose the best route, BGP performs an ordered evaluation of attributes to make a single, deterministic best-path decision. This design gives network operators policy control: by changing attributes before export or on import, you influence route selection without changing physical topology. A concrete example is comparing two routes to the same prefix: one route might have a higher LOCAL_PREF but a shorter AS_PATH, and Junos will evaluate LOCAL_PREF before AS_PATH so the higher LOCAL_PREF wins. A common misconception is to treat MED like LOCAL_PREF; they are not interchangeable. LOCAL_PREF is internal — it controls how your AS sends traffic out — while MED is a suggestion you give to a neighbor to influence how they send traffic into your AS. Remember also that some attributes are well-known and mandatory, such as NEXT_HOP and AS_PATH, while others are optional. The essential takeaway is that attributes are your policy knobs; use them carefully and verify with route detail commands.

AS_PATH is a well-known mandatory attribute containing the ordered list of autonomous systems a route traversed. Its two most important operational roles are loop prevention and path-length comparison. Loop prevention is simple: if a BGP speaker sees its own AS in the AS_PATH, it discards the route. For preference, Junos treats shorter AS_PATHs as more desirable after LOCAL_PREF checks have been performed. A concrete example: if a route comes with AS_PATH [65010 65020] and another with [65030], and both have equal LOCAL_PREF, the path with AS_PATH length one is preferred. Operators often use AS-path prepending to intentionally lengthen the AS_PATH when advertising to a peer, making that export less attractive to remote networks. The common pitfall here is overusing prepending without verification — excessive prepending can push traffic through unexpected intermediaries or create asymmetry. Always verify the effect by asking the peer to show received routes or by using public BGP looking glass tools. On Junos, you implement prepending in an export policy with an as-path-prepend action. The closing takeaway: use AS_PATH and prepending as a coarse remote steering tool and verify changes from the remote perspective.

NEXT_HOP is a well-known mandatory attribute that tells routers which IP address to forward packets to for a given prefix. The first criterion in Junos' best-path selection is that the NEXT_HOP must be reachable via an active route in the local routing table. If the next-hop is unreachable, the BGP route is considered invalid regardless of other attractive attributes. For eBGP neighbors, the next-hop is typically the peer's address. For iBGP paths, NEXT_HOP is usually preserved from the originating eBGP advertisement, which means internal routers require IGP routes to that next-hop. A practical example: an iBGP-learned route points to a next-hop on a remote eBGP peer; if the IGP lacks a path to that next-hop, the route will not become eligible. A common operational mistake is to forget to redistribute or provide IGP reachability to eBGP next-hops when using iBGP. Verify NEXT_HOP reachability with show route and trace the IGP path. The takeaway: always confirm next-hop reachability before changing other attributes; it is the gate that determines whether the rest of the best-path sequence even runs. NEXT_HOP and reachability means a route with an unreachable next-hop is discarded; ensure igp reachability for ibgp next-hops.. In practical terms, why next-hop reachability is the first gating check. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

LOCAL_PREF is a well-known discretionary attribute exchanged only among iBGP peers in the same AS. Its role is to signal which exit point the local AS prefers for outbound traffic. A higher LOCAL_PREF value is preferred, and it is evaluated early in the Junos best-path selection sequence after next-hop reachability. For example, if your AS has two eBGP peers to different ISPs and you set LOCAL_PREF 200 on routes learned from ISP A and leave ISP B at the default 100, all routers in your AS will prefer ISP A as the exit point for those prefixes. Practically, you implement this by creating an import policy that assigns local-preference and applying it to the BGP group. Mistakes often stem from applying the policy on the wrong direction: LOCAL_PREF must be applied on import to influence how you accept routes, not on export. Another pitfall is thinking LOCAL_PREF affects how neighbors choose paths into your AS — it does not. That is the role of MED or AS-path prepending. The takeaway: LOCAL_PREF is your authoritative internal stick for choosing an exit; use import policies and verify with show route protocol bgp.

MED, the Multi-Exit Discriminator, is an optional, non-transitive attribute used to tell a neighboring AS which entry point into your AS it should prefer. Unlike LOCAL_PREF, which controls outbound traffic inside your AS, MED is a suggestion for the adjacent AS about inbound traffic. Lower MED values are preferred. MED is typically exchanged between eBGP neighbors and is compared only among routes learned from the same adjacent AS by default on Junos. A concrete scenario: if you have two links to the same ISP AS, advertise a lower MED on the link you want that ISP to use as the primary entry. On Junos you set MED with the metric action in a policy prior to export. A common mistake is expecting MED to override LOCAL_PREF; it cannot. MED only affects the remote AS's decision, and how the remote AS evaluates MED depends on its own policies and configuration. Also remember MED is not transitive, so it won't propagate further beyond the immediate neighbor. The practical takeaway is to use MED when you want to influence a specific neighbor's inbound choice, and always test by checking the neighbor's received routes or asking them to report the decision.

ORIGIN indicates how a route entered BGP and serves as an early tie-breaker in the best-path selection. There are three origin codes: IGP, EGP, and Incomplete. IGP, marked as 'i', means the route was originated within the local AS using a network statement. EGP, 'e', is historical and rarely used. Incomplete, '?', indicates the route was redistributed into BGP from another source such as an IGP or static route. In Junos, the origin preference order is IGP first, then EGP, then Incomplete. This means that, after LOCAL_PREF and AS_PATH comparisons, a route tagged as IGP will beat one tagged as Incomplete. A practical example is when you redistribute static routes into BGP: those often become Incomplete and will be less preferred than routes that were originated via a BGP network statement. A common operator mistake is not understanding how redistribution changes origin and then being surprised when an internally originated route loses to an externally learned route. The takeaway: maintain clear origin semantics in your policy design and use explicit network statements when you want an IGP origin preference. ORIGIN attribute explained means origin signals how a route entered bgp; igp-originated routes are preferred over redistributed (incomplete) routes.. In practical terms, how origin type affects route preference. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Junos follows a strict, step-by-step process to select a single best BGP path when multiple paths exist. The first check is next-hop reachability: if the next-hop is not in the routing table the path is discarded. Next, Junos compares LOCAL_PREF and prefers the path with the highest value, which is why operators use LOCAL_PREF to control outbound behavior. If LOCAL_PREF is equal, Junos prefers the shorter AS_PATH. If AS_PATH lengths are equal, the ORIGIN code is evaluated with preference order IGP, EGP, and then Incomplete. MED comes next: Junos prefers the lower MED but, by default, compares MED only among routes learned from the same adjacent AS. If MED is equal or not comparable, Junos prefers eBGP-learned paths over iBGP. For iBGP-learned routes, it then considers the IGP cost to reach the BGP next-hop and prefers the lower cost. Remaining tie-breakers are lowest Router ID and, finally, lowest peer IP address. A concrete example: two routes with equal LOCAL_PREF and reachable next-hops will be compared by AS_PATH length and origin next. A frequent misconception is that MED always wins over AS_PATH; it does not. The right sequence helps you predict outcomes and design policies accordingly.

Routing policies in Junos let you modify attributes at import or export time to control how routes are accepted or advertised. The direction matters: an import policy alters attributes of routes you receive before they enter your RIB, while an export policy changes attributes before you send routes to a neighbor. Use import policies to set LOCAL_PREF for routes learned from a peer so internal routers prefer or avoid that path. Use export policies to set MED or prepend AS numbers before advertising to a neighbor when you want to influence their decisions. For example, to prefer ISP A for outbound traffic, create an import policy that sets local-preference 200 and apply it to the group receiving routes from ISP A. To make ISP B less preferred externally, create an export policy that prepends your AS twice and apply it to the group for ISP B. A common operator error is applying a LOCAL_PREF change as an export action expecting remote peers to change their behavior — LOCAL_PREF is only exchanged internally, so it must be applied on import. Always validate policy effects with show route protocol bgp detail and, for export effects, ask the neighbor to run show route receive-protocol or check a looking glass if available. The operational lesson: direction and the attribute's scope determine which policy type to use.

Several repeatable mistakes cause unexpected BGP behavior. First, confusing LOCAL_PREF and MED leads operators to apply the wrong policy direction: LOCAL_PREF affects outbound decisions inside your AS and is set on import; MED is exported to neighbors to influence inbound choice. Second, failing to ensure IGP reachability to BGP next-hops causes iBGP-learned routes to be invalid even if attributes are attractive. Third, applying an import policy when you intended export will silently change attribute visibility and can cause route loss or asymmetry. Finally, excessive AS-path prepending without verification can shift traffic to unintended intermediate providers and make troubleshooting harder. For troubleshooting, start with next-hop verification: run show route protocol bgp detail and confirm the next-hop is present in the routing table. Then inspect LOCAL_PREF and AS_PATH in the same output to see why a different path may have been selected. If you changed export behavior, ask the neighbor to show their received routes or use a looking glass to validate the effect. The practical habit is to make single changes, verify with show outputs, and have rollback steps ready. That disciplined approach prevents prolonged outages or blackholes.

This hands-on scenario asks you to influence outbound traffic toward ISP A and make ISP B prefer a different path into your network. The network has R1 in AS 65000 peered to R2 (ISP A, AS 100) and R3 (ISP B, AS 200). To prefer ISP A for outbound traffic, create an import policy on R1 that sets local-preference 200 for routes learned from R2, and ensure that policy is attached to the BGP group receiving routes from ISP A. For inbound control toward R3, create an export policy that prepends your AS twice so the path appears longer to ISP B and remote peers. The lesson includes the canonical Junos snippets: set policy-options policy-statement PREFER_ISP_A term 1 then local-preference 200 and set policy-options policy-statement PREPEND_AS_TO_ISP_B term 1 then as-path-prepend "65000 65000". Configure the BGP groups to use these policies on import or export as appropriate. After applying changes, verify with show route protocol bgp detail on R1 to confirm LOCAL_PREF and AS_PATH. Also check R3's received view via show route receive-protocol bgp if you can. A common error is forgetting to advertise the local prefix or forgetting to provide IGP reachability to next-hops; verify the static route or network configuration used to originate the test prefix. This exercise reinforces the import/export distinction and the verification steps.

These three concepts capture the essentials you will use daily. First, AS_PATH is both loop prevention and a length metric; shorter AS_PATHs are preferred after LOCAL_PREF. Second, NEXT_HOP reachability is the gatekeeper: an unreachable next-hop makes a path invalid regardless of other attributes. Third, LOCAL_PREF is the authoritative internal mechanism to control outbound routing; it must be set on import and is seen only inside your AS. Keep these three in mind when you read show route output or design simple policies: verify next-hop before attribute comparisons, set LOCAL_PREF where you want to control internal exit selection, and use AS_PATH prepending carefully to influence remote choices. These quick reminders help you reason about why Junos picks one path instead of another and avoid common operational mistakes. A few more compact reminders will keep your operations safe. First, MED is a neighbor-facing suggestion for inbound traffic; lower values are preferred but only apply to the receiving AS's decision. Second, the Junos best-path algorithm is sequential and deterministic: if you know the order, you can predict how small attribute changes will shift traffic. Third, policy direction is critical: import policies alter attributes you accept and are used for LOCAL_PREF; export policies change attributes you send and are used for MED and AS-path prepending. When making changes, implement one change at a time, verify with show route protocol bgp and peer-received views, and maintain rollback configurations. These short, repeatable rules reduce the risk of policy errors and make debugging faster.
